paras: The Elm Bottom lynching report of 1882 was a widely circulated account that the bodies of four men, two hanged and two shot, had been found in the Elm bottom of Denton County, Texas, on the morning of June 22, 1882. Wire dispatches from Dallas presented the deaths as a lynching of cowboys or cattle thieves, and the story ran in papers from California to New Hampshire. The Dallas Daily Herald, the nearest paper in the coverage, doubted the rumor from the start and the next day called it a hoax.

According to the Dallas Herald, the place was in the Elm bottom near the Missouri Pacific line north of Lewisville; the San Antonio Evening Light placed it between Denton and Pilot Point, and the wire named it as near "Platt Point" or "Platte Point." The Herald linked the rumor to a man named Carter, said to be a relative of "Carter of Sam Bass fame," who had been captured the Tuesday night before while trying to rob a Missouri Pacific passenger train several miles from Denton.

The Herald's account came second-hand: a young man, C. W. Halsell, brought the story to Dallas from Mrs. McWorter, who lived near Lewisville. In that version two men hung by their necks from limbs and two others, about half a mile away, had been shot; all were "dressed in cow-boy style" and none was identified, though one was said to have been seen the previous day at Caruth's ranch nearby. The Evening Light's Dallas dispatch said a farmer found the bodies, two hanging from a limb with their "comrades" beneath them shot in the forehead, and that they were recognized as men suspected of stock theft.
No source names any of the dead, and none states their race. The killers were not identified; one brief said the men were supposed to have been hanged by "victimized stockmen."

On June 24 the Dallas Herald printed a single line among its local items saying that the report of four men found dead in Elm bottom "turns out to be a hoax." No report of an inquest, identification, arrest or further explanation appears in the coverage.

Outside Dallas the story spread as fact through a Dallas wire dated June 23, carried the next day under headlines such as "Four Men Lynched" in the Wheeling Register, "Four Victims of Lynch Law" in the Sacramento Record-Union and "Four Cowboys Found Dead" in the Memphis Appeal. The Wheeling Register's version closed, "No doubt they were lynched for stealing cattle," and the Evening Light treated the deaths lightly, saying their "sudden demise" was traceable to carelessness with "other people's stock."

As the item was condensed for weekly news columns its details drifted: the dead became "horse thieves" in New Hampshire, and in Dakota and Michigan papers "three cattle thieves" found hanging to a tree. A Kentucky paper folded the case into a remark on hangings that day, "Nine in one day is doing pretty well." Digest briefs in Mississippi and Louisiana repeated the story without qualification on July 1 and July 15, well after the Herald's retraction, and no correction appears in any paper outside Dallas.

Whether the killings happened at all is the central dispute: the wire stated them as fact, while the Herald reported that the Denton mail agent had heard nothing of any bodies and then called the story a hoax. The Herald was the closest source and the only one that reported checking the story, which gives its doubt more weight than the distant reprints. The accounts also differ on the number of dead (four or three), the county (Denton or "Benton"), and whether all the bodies were hanging or only two.
